label: August 1890
atlas_dek: The episodes of anti-Black violence reported in August 1890 from our dossiers, placed on 1890 county lines and by month (some July events were first reported in August). Hover for a short summary; select a dot to read the account in the sidebar. Drafts: no entry has had human review.
reader_intro:
Dossiers for 37 episodes of anti-Black violence reported in August 1890. They come from the 72 located events in the August 1890 table, which includes July events first reported in August, plus the lynching of Jim Robinson near Shaw, Mississippi, which the first search missed because his only report sat on an undivided LoC-only page of the Greenville Times, and four events found by a check of every August article for attacks by one person. We did not write dossiers for eight events that were plainly out of scope from the table alone: the lynching of Charles Pratt at Blair, Nebraska, who was white; a Mexican man lynched at Shafter, Texas, months earlier; two near-hangings with no Black person involved (Bairdstown, Ohio, and Racine, Wisconsin); a legal hanging at Rocky Mount, Virginia; a second record of the Early Holt shooting; and two editorial references to old killings with no date. Eleven more belong to other months, among them the riot on a Black excursion at Camilla, Georgia, about July 25, the fish-pond riot in Fayette County, Georgia, at the end of July, and the police killing of John Walton at Houston on July 28. Searches covered August papers, plus September papers for more on known episodes. For 1890 the search used white papers only: the Black-press collection holds only scattered issues for this year.

Sixteen of the 53 dossiers are set aside. William Sloan, reported lynched near Vicksburg, was jailed according to the Grenada Sentinel. The Jackson, Mississippi, cannon demonstration comes from testimony about an earlier election. No report gives anyone’s race in four cases (Armistead Huff in Oglethorpe County, Georgia; John Bruce at Brandenburg, Kentucky; Stapleton Notlepass at Muncie, Indiana; and Strother, whipped by Indiana white caps). In four others no racial motive appears: a fight among Black workers at the Shelby Iron Works in Alabama, a brawl at the Charleston, West Virginia, Republican convention, and two shootings by robbers or burglars. Two manhunts harmed no Black person, two fights were two-sided (Alexandria, Virginia, and a train near Coal City, Ohio), and two cases involved no force: a walkout of white packers at Nashville and a threat to a Black preacher’s credentials over his vote at Glenville, Arkansas.

Police violence is kept generously: men shot while fleeing or resisting arrest are included, and only gunfights over a crime in progress are set aside from the totals. Peonage, force used to hold a Black worker to labor, is always included; a search of August papers found no case. Where an inventory’s race differs from the press, the entry keeps the inventory and states the difference.

Attacks by one person: our definition covers violence by groups and by people acting with public authority, so an attack by a single private person is normally left out. A check of every August article for such attacks added the shooting of George Carter in King George County, Virginia, after a political quarrel, a sidewalk clash at Rome, Georgia, and two assaults at Americus, Georgia, all kept and marked as one-person attacks.

Method: a research agent (Sonnet) searched the papers. A write-up agent (Opus) wrote the dossier with keyed citations, and a code check confirmed every quote and citation against the article text. White-press clippings are page images where we could place them on the scan, otherwise text.

Drafts: no entry has had human review.
